This is the other side of the coin, and I completely agree. I can watch 50+ people on my feed absolutely print, but if my own trades aren’t gaining traction, why the heck would I press?

You've heard me say it a million times, but my current/open positions are my feedback loop.

If I’m taking scratches, getting stopped, or nothing is following through, I size down, go back to pilots, and eventually just sit on my hands. I don’t need to make the market pay me because somebody else is making money.

July is a perfect example. @FranVezz and I were very prominent and vocal about our sitting, and we've now reaped the rewards from sitting in July! I was mostly cash and barely did anything, while a lot of people chopped themselves to death trying to create opportunity that just didn't exist.

Then August + September came around, my setups started working again, positions gained traction, and I had the mental & monetary capital to press when my feedback loop told me to.

I like to think of it like poker... just because everyone else at the table is throwing chips around doesn’t mean I suddenly have a good hand.

My cards determine how I bet!!

There’s a subtle difference between a stock "holding support" and buyers actually defending support.

And learning to recognize it has saved me a LOT of bad entries in the past.

Demand should actually look like demand, right? If price slowly bleeds into my 9/21EMA, prior breakout, gap, etc. and then just sits at LOD for 30-60 minutes with sellers leaning on it, I’m probably not interested... I want buyers to respond with some urgency.

The longer price sits on support without bouncing, the more I assume supply (sellers) are chewing through the demand (buyers).

Analogies help me a lot. Think of support like a floor taking repeated hammer blows... if every hit gets absorbed but nobody pushes price back up, eventually the floor cracks. It's simple.

That’s why I’d rather see the flush, sharp rejection, right-side curl, VWAP/15-30min pivot reclaim before putting risk on. I don’t buy a level because my line says demand should exist there.

I want aggressive buyers to actually show up!!

I genuinely have no clue how long I will hold a stock when I enter an idea.

I could get stopped out 5 minutes later or still be holding it weeks later. I define my risk, let price action confirm/deny the thesis, and manage the position accordingly. I’m not entering at the open saying, “This is a 4day swing,” because price hasn’t earned that decision yet.

Especially in this environment, I try my best to let a day trade earn the right to become a swing trade, then let the swing earn the right to become a position trade.

If I build enough cushion into EOD, I’ll swing it overnight, reassess the next session, trail against my pivots/9&21EMAs, and repeat for as long as the thesis remains intact.

Long story short, I don’t decide the holding period... price does.

This is basically the only way I’ve learned to survive a truly "choppy" market.

I stopped paying up through pivots and started buying against them. There’s a BIG difference between chop and a healthy trending environment.

In healthy markets, I’m comfortable buying through pivots because momentum gets sustained, but in chop, those same breakouts love to shake your hand and immediately steal your wallet.

My entry tactics change depending on the current environment + I have many resources on my page about this very concept... I’m still focused on leaders + major pivots, but in chop I’d much rather buy the flush into the 9/21EMA, prior breakout, gap, etc., wait for the right-side curl/VWAP reclaim, and define risk against LOD.

Environment decides how aggressive I get, while location keeps my risk tight.

& repeat until conditions improve.

It took me way too long to realize the thing I thought was making me a better trader was actually making me worse.

For the first 2+ years, I kept adding more. Another indicator, setup, another timeframe, chasing alerts, rules + another trader’s opinion. I thought knowing more meant I was improving, but really I was just giving myself 10 different reasons to second-guess every decision I made intraday.

Eventually I started deleting as much as possible, and weirdly enough, that’s when my trading got 10x better.

I'm such a simple man now. I’d rather understand 3 things at a stupidly deep level than know a little bit about 20+. Give me leading stocks, daily/weekly pivots, price/volume + defined risk, and I can basically build my entire trading process around that.

1 of my favorite quotes, by the legend himself...

"I fear not the man who has practiced 10,000 kicks once, but I fear the man who has practiced one kick 10,000 times." - Bruce Lee

I think that’s the uncomfortable part nobody talks about, but simplicity takes conviction. It’s easy to keep adding because adding feels like progress. It’s much harder to figure out what actually makes you money, throw the rest in the trash, and do the same boring stuff 1,000 times every single day.

The longer I trade, the less I seem to need.
